docs.title: General Pipeline
docs.text:
Welcome to MOCHA. MOCHA aims to build a joint analysis pipeline for multi-modal/contrast/sequence (collectively referred to as multi-sequence for simplicity) vascular images, including:

  • Registration of multi-sequence 3D images
  • Centerline tracing using VesselVoyager.
  • Extraction of 2D multi-sequence cross-sectional images based on the vessel centerlines and registered images
  • Manual or AI-based tissue segmentation (contour labeling) on 2D cross-sectional images using MOCHA Viewer.
  • Feature measurements and statistical analysis based on segmentations.

We develop VesselVoyager and MOCHA Viewer software to facilitate the above operations.

docs.title: Windows 10 or higher
docs.text:
VIL members: download the software through the MS Teams channel.

Outside users: please contact Xin Wang at xwang99[at]uw[dot]edu for more information.

docs.text: Please contact Xin Wang at xwang99[at]uw[dot]edu for a workable version of the software on these operating systems.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: MOCHA Viewer is for contour labeling on 2D cross-sectional images generated from vessel centerlines.

docs.title: AI Prediction
docs.text: You can use AI to preform automated contour labeling.

docs.title: Lumen and outer wall segmentation
docs.text:
Currently, we support to predict "Lumen" and "Outer Wall" contours. To do so, click the menubar, AI → Lumen/Wall Seg, then a prompt window will appear

Here, you can select one single image sequence to perform the prediction. For best performance, it is recommended to use pre-contrast T1 or a similar sequence.

You can choose to only predict contours for those slice without lumen or outer wall contours through a check box. It is checked by default.

You can determine the range of slices to predict by changing the values in the two text boxes. The default range is all the slices (from the first to the last one).

Once the options are good, click OK and wait for seconds. The predicted lumen and outer wall contours will appear.

docs.title: CE map
docs.text:
Contrast enhancement (CE) map can be visualized once Lumen and Outer Wall contours are labeled. To show the CE map, in the menubar click Analysis → CE Map.

A prompt window (shown below) will ask you to specify the image sequences corresponding to pre- and post-contrast T1. Also, for each T1 (pre or post), you need to specify a normalization parameter that is used to normalize the image intensity. Then, click OK, and wait a few seconds.

The CE map will appear in an additional image sequence window (shown below). The map is only valid in the outer wall area, as defined by the contours. For other region, the post contrast T1 image will be shown. The color bar indicates the correspondence between the pixel colors of the map and the enhancement values. You can hover your mouse on the map to see the enhancement value of the pixel at the lower right corner. You can also enable the MPR view of the CE map.

By clicking Analysis → CE Map* in the menu bar again, you can hide the CE map window. If you want to update the CE map (for example, after changing the contours or shifts of slices), hide the CE map and show it again by clicking the same menubar button.

docs.title: V1.6.0
docs.text:
Functionality:

Users can specify the contour type, layer spacing, number of layers, and operations (expand and/or shrink original contours). Results will be saved in the folder "multilayer_masks" which is a subfolder of the opened vessel folder.

Bug fixes:

  • Fixed the bug that sometimes the slice indices in contour.yaml are saved as np.int32 rather than int, causing nonsense characters.
  • For DCE analysis, multiply Kp by 5 when calculating V-V images to align with 2D CASCADE.

docs.text:
Bug fix:

  • Fixed the bug that the software cannot read the cross-sectional image folder if there exist two image sequences where one name is xxx and the other name also ends with xxx.

docs.title: V1.5.0
docs.text:
Functionality:

  • Undo and redo. Use Ctrl+Z or Ctrl+Y to undo or redo an operation. The operation can be editing a contour or shifting a slice. "Apply Shift" can also be undone or redone.
  • Load contours from a segmentation file. Click the menubar, "Contour" -> "Load from Seg" to select the segmentation file to load. After loading, one can optionally clean all previous contours of a loaded contour type in the prompt window.
  • Mark the reference slice. By default the first slice is the reference slice. To set another slice as the reference slice, go to that slice, then click the menubar, "Show" -> "Set Ref. Slice". The reference slice has a relative index of 0, and other slices have relative indices of positive or negative numbers, depending on the relative location to the reference slice. The relative index is shown in a textbox of the left panel, next to the slice index textbox. One can type a number in the text box to quickly go to the slice with the corresponding relative index.
  • Hotkey settings. Click the menubar, "Settings" -> "Hotkeys" to check all hotkeys. One can customize the hotkeys in the prompt window. The hotkeys will be saved for each Windows user account.
  • Add two endpoints handles to the line segment in the cross-sectional slice window in the MPR mode to enable moving the line segment.

UI:

  • When the mouse hovers over a contour or its key point, the corresponding item will be highlighted to indicate that it can be clicked.
  • Selected text box will be highlighted with an orange border.
  • Click the menubar, "Help"->"User Manual" to see software instructions.

Bug fixes:

  • Fix the bug that the intensity information in the lower right corner of the cross-sectional image window does not account for the image offset.
  • Fix the bug that the shown slice is incorrect when the number entered into the slice index textbox is smaller than 1 or larger than the number of slices.
  • Fix the bug that visualizing 3D centerlines requires a 3D image file named exactly as "TOF.nii.gz". Now any ".nii.gz" file in the parent folder of the "xsec" folder can be detected.
  • Fix the bug that the contour width will become smaller after one clicks outside the contour on the image.
  • Fix the bug that when one starts to drag a contour key point and the initial speed is too large, dragging will fail.
  • Fix the bug that when one starts to drag a contour key point, there is a delay before the point starts moving.

docs.title: V1.4.1
docs.text:
Bug fix:

docs.title: V1.4.0
docs.text:
Functionality

  • Apply the shift (a.k.a. offset, or manual registration) of current slice of an image sequence to other slices (user specified), by menubar, Show-Apply Shift.
  • When rotating the line segment on the cross-sectional window to change the MPR view, the MPR views of all image sequences are synchronized. In other words, the line segments for rotation behave in the same way when each of them is rotated.
  • The number of key points of the contours predicted by AI is reduced to a half of the previous number. Therefore, users can modify the contours more conveniently.

UI

  • Show the axial, sagittal, coronal views of original 3D images (if exists) in a separate tab on the left side. The views correspond to the spatial location (in original space) of currently shown cross-sectional slices.
  • When extracting cross-sections from a VesselVoyager folder, users can select image sequences and specify the height and width of the cross-sections (200 by default).
  • Open a MOCHA folder or a VesselVoyager folder using the same menubar button: File-Open Folder.

Bug fix:

  • The MPR views now respect the shifts of different slices. (Previously, the MPR views were based only on the nii images, and did not consider manual registration via the Shift button.)
  • When extracting cross-sections from a VesselVoyager folder, the points of interpolated centerlines now have (nearly) equal distance (1 pixel).

docs.text:

docs.title: V1.0.0
docs.text: • Initial release

docs.title: Contour Labeling
docs.text:
The key function of this software is to label contours on images. Each contour has a type name (such as "Lumen" or "Outer Wall"). Each type of contours has the same color if shown.

A contour contains a closed curve and several key points (figure below). The curve is determined by the key points through a smooth B-spline curve interpolation. You can control the shape of the contour by controlling those key points, such as moving their locations, adding or deleting key points.

The tools for contour labeling are in a table (figure below) on the left panel. Each row corresponds to a contour type.

By default, all contours are hidden after opening the software. To show all contours of a certain type, you can check the checkbox in the show column and the row corresponding to that contour type. For example, the status of the checkboxes in the above figure indicates that the "Lumen" and "Outer Wall" contours are shown, while the "Calcification" contours (if exist) are hidden.

docs.title: Draw new contours
docs.text:
To draw a new contour, you can first activate the contour drawing mode by clicking the button in the draw column and the row corresponding to that contour type. The button will become blue, showing the activation status. Another alternative way is to press the number key corresponding to the contour type. For example, to activate drawing "Lumen" contours, just press 1.

Once the drawing mode is activated, you can click a location in a image sequence window to add a key point. Click multiple times to add multiple keypoints.

Once you think the newly added keypoints are sufficient, click the previous button in the draw column, or press the number key again to deactivate the drawing mode. A curve will be automatically generated to represented the contour based on the keypoints.

The pipeline "activate drawing mode" - "add key points" - "deactivate drawing mode" will generate one single contour. If you want to draw another contour, then perform this pipeline again.

Same contour for all image sequences

If you draw a contour on one sequence, after finishing drawing, the same contour will appear on all sequence. This is similar to 2D CASCADE. This implies you are drawing contours based on all the sequences.

Minimum number of key points

You need to add at least three key points in order to generate a contour. If the number of newly added key points is less than 3 when you deactivate the drawing mode, all key points will be removed and no contour will be generated.

Drawing mode is exclusive for one contour type

The drawing mode can only be activated for one single contour type at the same time. If you have activated the drawing mode for type 1 (e.g., "Lumen"), and then activate the drawing mode for type 2 (e.g., "Outer Wall"), the drawing mode for type 1 will be automatically deactivated, and any key points you have added after activating the drawing mode for type 1 will be used to generate a contour of type 1.

Automatically showing contours after activating drawing mode

If you activate drawing mode for type 1 contour, and you haven't checked the checkbox in the show column for type 1, then this checkbox will automatically be checked and all existing type 1 contours will show. The logic here is that you cannot draw a type 1 contour if you have hidden type 1.

In contrast, if you uncheck a checkbox in the draw column before you deactivate the drawing mode for the same contour type, the drawing mode will be automatically deactivated, and a new contour will be generated (if there are more than three newly added key points) and then hidden.

docs.title: Change contour shape
docs.text: You can drag a key point on a contour in an image sequence window, and then the shape of the contour curve will change accordingly in real time in all image sequence windows. This is useful to adjust the shape of an existing contour, without deleting it and drawing a new one.

docs.title: Select contours or key points
docs.text:
You can click on an existing contour (but not on a key point) to select that contour. The selected contours are highlighted with a white color and a slightly thicker width.

You can click on a key point to select it. The selected key points are highlighted with a white color.

You cannot select a contours and a key point at the same time.

docs.title: Delete existing contours or key points
docs.text:
To delete an existing contour, just select it and then press Del. The contour curve and key points will be removed and this operation cannot be undone.

To delete an existing key point, just select it and then press Del. The selected key points will be removed, and the contour curve will be regenerated based on the rest of the key points. This is useful if you think the key points are too many.

docs.title: Add key points to existing contours
docs.text: You can add a key point to an existing contour, by Ctrl + clicking any location on the contour. A key point will be added at that location, and the contour curve will be regenerated based on all key points (including the new one).

docs.title: Expand or shrink contours
docs.text: You can spatially expand or shrink selected contours by pressing the keys = or -. All the key points will move along the normal vectors of the contour accordingly.

docs.title: Move contours
docs.text: You can spatially translate selected contours by pressing the arrow keys Up, Down, Left or Right.

docs.title: Copy and paste contours
docs.text: You can copy selected contours by Ctrl + C. You can then navigate to another slice, and paste those contours by Ctrl + V. Note that if there exists the same contour, then pasting will not perform.

docs.title: Change colors or type names
docs.text: You can click a color block in the color column to change the color of the corresponding contour type in a prompt window. You can also double-click a table cell in the type column to change the corresponding contour type name. Note that you cannot change it to a name that has been used by another contour type (a prompt window will show this information if you try to do that).

docs.title: Add new types
docs.text: You can add a new contour type. To do so, in the menubar click Contour → Add New Type, then a new row will appear in the contour table. The default name of the new contour type is "tmp*", you may change the name and the color to make it fit the need.

docs.title: Delete contour types
docs.text:
You can delete a contour type from the contour table, and in this way, all the existing contours (no matter whether they are visible) of this type will be deleted. To do so, just click the corresponding row in the table to select the row, then in the menubar click Contour → Delete Selected Types, then click yes in the prompt window.

Do NOT delete the default contour types.

There are some default contour types defined by 2D CASCADE. They will all appear in the contour table, even if there is no corresponding contour labels on the opened images.

To avoid potential confilcts and bugs occured by CASCADE, the following things are not recommended:

  • Delete a default contour type.
  • Add a new contour type with a name similar to the name of a default contour type.
  • Change the color of a default contour type.

The default types are: 'Lumen', 'Outer Wall', 'Calcification', 'Necrotic/Lipid Core', 'Loose Matrix', 'Type I Hemorrhage', 'Type II Hemorrhage', 'Ulcer', 'Thrombus', 'Other Types', 'Fibrous', 'Fibrous - CA', 'Fibrous - LM', 'Lipid Accumulation', 'Hemorrhage Out Core', 'ECA Lumen': '187', 'ECA Wall', 'Shoulder', 'Muscle', 'Vesselwall Centerline'.

Warning

The operation of deleting a contour type cannot be undone. All information of the contour type will be lost, including the shape and position of each contour and the color and name of the contour type. If you regret after deleting a contour type, then you need to close the software without saving to prevent the results from being saved.

docs.title: Data Saving
docs.text:
Saving back to a 2D CASCADE folder

This tool is under active development and may have some bugs that could destroy the original CASCADE data if the opened folder is a 2D CASCADE folder. So before saving, it is strongly recommended that you back up all the QVJ and QVS files in the CASCADE folder. The dicom files do not need to be backed up. If the opened folder is a MOCHA or VesseyVoyager folder, no back up is needed also.

You can press Ctrl+S or click save button (figure below) on the left panel to save current results back to the opened folder. An alternative way is to click the menubar, File → Save.

When saving the data, a message and a progress bar will appear in the status bar at the bottom of the software window to indicate the progress. Once saving is finished (usually in 0.5 seconds), the progress bar will disappear, and the message will show "finished":

New in V1.1.0

When closing the software window, a prompt window (figure below) will ask whether you want to save results before closing. Click one of the buttons:

  • Yes: save results and then close the software.
  • No: discard unsaved results, and then close the software.
  • Cancel: do not save results, nor close the software. In other words, nothing will happen.

docs.title: Image Display
docs.text: The displayed images are indicated by the red box in the figure below:

docs.title: Basic information
docs.text:
Each image sequence is show in one individual window.

  • Path of the opened folder is show at the top.
  • Index of the shown slice and the total number of slices are shown in the upper left corner of each cross-section window.
  • Sequence names are shown in the upper right corner of each cross-section window.
  • Pixel indices (in row and column) that the mouse is hovering over are shown in the lower left corner of the cross-section window.
  • Pixel intensity that the mouse is hovering over is shown in the lower right corner of the cross-section window. (Note that if the window is for the contrast-enhancement map, CE map, then the shown intensity is for the map rather than the post-contrast image.)
  • Image boundary is indicated by four blue lines (two horizontal and two vertical).

docs.title: Show or hide sequences
docs.text: To show or hide an image sequence, click the menubar, Show → Sequences → {seq}, where {seq} is the name of the sequence you want to show or hide. Names of currently shown sequences are with check marks.

docs.title: Pan and zoom
docs.text:
When the Pan button (figure below) in the left panel is activated (by default), you can:

  • Drag mouse in any sequence window to pan (move) the image.
  • Scroll up/down when the mouse is in any sequence window to zoom in/out.

Note that all the sequence windows will behave in the same way as you pan or zoom. In other words, the viewing range of the images of all sequences is synchronized automatically.

At any time, you can click the Rescale Button (figure below) to immediately rescale all images to their original viewing range. This is useful if you accidentally pan or zoom too much and want to recover.

docs.title: Navigate to another slice
docs.text:
The sequence windows only show one same slice for each sequence. To change the shown slice, you can use one of the following ways:

  • Press Q or E to move to the previous or next slice.
  • Press Shift + Q or E to move to the previous or next slice that has contours of shown contour types.
  • Type an integer in the textbox of slice index (figure below). When you are typing in a textbox, you can also press Up or Down to increase or decrease the number.

docs.title: Change intensity windows
docs.text:
The intensity windows for each sequence are shown as a table in the left panel:

The table contains the following information:

  • Sequence names.
  • Min and max values of the intensity windows.

Note that the min/max values have a relationship with the window level and width:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{min}=\text{Level}-\frac{\text{Width}}{2}\\ \text{max}=\text{Level}+\frac{\text{Width}}{2} \end{aligned} \]

When the Drag Control button is activated, you can drag your mouse in any sequence window to change the window level/width of that image sequence. The behavior is the same as the Radiant software for viewing Dicom images. Specifically:

  • Drag up/down to increase/decrease window level.
  • Drag right/left to increase/decrease window width.

You can also click the default button to reset the intensity window of each sequence. The default window is the range from the 1st to 99th percentile of the intensity distribution.

docs.title: Image rendering mode
docs.text:
By default, the images are rendered through nearest-neighbor interpolation. As a result, you may observe clear square-like boundaries between adjacent pixels. To view images under a smooth mode, click the menubar, Settings → Smooth Image, then the images are rendered through linear interpolation, like other software such as 2D CASCADE and Radiant. To change the mode back, click it again.

A comparison between the two modes:

Recommended mode

The nearest-neighbor mode is recommended and thus activated by default. This is because it shows the real appearance of the original image, which is essentially a discrete grid of pixels. The clear boundaries between adjacent pixels in this mode could help better identify the boundary of tissues, leading to a more accurate manual contour labeling.

docs.title: Manually register images
docs.text:
Theoretically, all the sequences have been registered (spatially aligned) before using this software. However, there could be non-perfect registration, such that you may observe structure misalignment of certain cross-sectional slices.

2D CASCADE provides a tool to manually move (translate) a slice of one sequence such that it can better align with other sequences. To do so in this software, click the Shift button to activate the manual registration mode:

Then you can drag in any sequence window to move that slice. Once you finish, remember to deactivate the registration mode by clicking the button again. The resulting slice could look like:

Note that when you register the slice by dragging, the image will be moved, but the blue lines indicating the image boundary will be fixed.

After shifting a slice, you can apply the shifting result to other slices of the same image sequence. To do so, in the menubar, click Show → Apply Shift. A prompt window (shown below) will ask you to select the image sequence and slice range.

For example, if the currently viewed slice is the 10th slice (indicated by the upper left corner in the cross-sectional image window), and in the prompt window you select TOF and a slice range from 50 to 60, then the shift of the 10th slice of TOF will be applied to the 50th to 60th slices of TOF. You can confirm the result by navigating to the corresponding slices.

docs.title: MPR views
docs.text:
There are theoretically two ways to view an image:

  • View the cross-sectional 2D slices.
  • View the longitudinal 2D slices, a.k.a. the MPR view.

By default, only the cross-sectional slices are shown. To also show the MPR view, click the MPR button (figure below). To hide the MPR view, click it again.

Then, the GUI will look like:

Key components include:

  • ① A red line segment that indicates the cropping direction corresponding to the MPR view. You can drag the small circle on the line segment to rotate it. You can also drag the small squares at the endpoints of the line segment, to move the line segment such that it will not go through the image center anymore. The MPR view will change according to the location and orientation of the line segment.
  • ② A horizontal blue line on each MPR window that indicates the current slice index. If you change the shown slice, this line will move accordingly.
  • ③ A splitter that can be dragged to change the heights of the cross-section and MPR windows.

Besides, clicking on any MPR image can automatically change the shown cross-sectional slice to the one corresponding to the clicked location.

docs.title: Centerline visualization
docs.text:
Suppose the opened folder is extracted from a VesselVoyager folder, i.e., if the folder structure is: 

folder_1
    - centerline.yaml
    - TOF.nii.gz
    - xsec
        - ICA_L-xxxxxx (opened folder)
where TOF and ICA_L are just example names for image sequences and vessels, respectively. Then the vessel centerline tree can be visualized. To do so, in the menubar clicking Show → Centerlines.

A separate window (shown below) will appear. Each vessel is shown in one color:

  • Orange: the vessel corresponding to the opened folder.
  • Blue: the vessels whose cross-sectional images are extracted, i.e., the vessels in the xsec folder.
  • Gray: the vessels whose cross-sections are not extracted.

There is also a red point on the orange (opened) vessel. This red point indicates the location of the currently viewed 2D cross-sectional slice in the vessel tree. If you navigate to another slice, this red point will update in real time.

docs.title: Original image views
docs.text:
If the opened folder is extracted from a VesselVoyager folder (see Centerline visualization in this page for more information), then you can view the original images by clicking the tab Original Img in the left panel:

Then the left panel will switch to three views (axial, sagittal, coronal) of an original image sequence. By default, no sequence is chosen when you view the tab for the first time. You can use the drop-down list to select a sequence:

Then, the three views will appear (for simplicity, only one view is shown below). The red cross-hair indicates the spatial location of the currently viewed cross-sectional slice in the original 3D image. If you navigate to another slice, three views will update in real time.

docs.title: Grid of dashed lines
docs.text:
If the Grid button (figure below) is activated, then a grid of dashed lines (figure below) is shown on every cross-sectional image window.

The grid of lines is useful if you want to know how good the alignment among image sequences is, because you can check tissue locations relative to the reference lines, and quickly notice whether the same tissue in another image sequence is at the same location. Due to its usefulness in checking alignment situation, when you activate the Shift button to perform a manual registration, the Grid button will be automatically activated. You can then deactivate it manually if you do not want to see the grid of lines.

docs.title: Folder format
docs.text:
The first step is to open a folder by the tool, such that images and contours (if exist) can be displayed.

The following types of folders are supported:

  • MOCHA folder: contains NIfTI (.nii.gz) files of MPR (cross-sectional) images,
  • VesselVoyager folder: contains NIfTI files of 3D images and a yaml file of centerline coordinates,
  • 2D CASCADE project folder: contains DICOM, .QVJ and .QVS files.

docs.title: MPR Image folder
docs.text:
The folder should contain NIfTI files of MPR (cross-sectional) images. Each file is named as xsec_{seq}.nii.gz or xsec_{whatever}_{seq}.nii.gz. Here, {seq} is any name that indicates the MR sequence name, such as S101 or pre-T1; {whatever} can be any name.

Restriction for {seq} and {whatever}

The only restriction: they should not contain the underline _.

To open a folder, click the menubar, File → Open Xsec Folder. Then select the folder you want to open. If multiple sequences are detected, a prompt window will ask you to select the sequences you want to show (figure below). By default, all sequences are selected.

docs.title: 3D Image folder
docs.text:
The folder should contain NIfTI files of 3D images. Each file is named as {seq}.nii.gz. Here, {seq} is any name that indicates the MR sequence name, such as TOF. The folder should also contain a centerline.yaml yaml file that contains centerline information following VesselVoyager's format.

(New in V2.0.0) The folder may also contain registration files named reg_{moving_seq}_to_{ref_seq}.txt, where {moving_seq} is the moving sequence and {ref_seq} is the reference sequence. If there is no registration file for a specific sequence, this sequence is assumed to be registered to the reference sequence already. As a special case, if there are no registration files, all sequences are assumed to be registered. For details about how to register sequences to generate these registration files, go to "Preprocessing" on the left table of content of this webpage, and then go to "Image Registration" section.

To open the 3D image folder, click the menubar, File → Open Folder. Then select the folder you want to open. A prompt window (figure below) will ask for the vessels (①) and image sequences (②) to extract, as well as the height and width (③, in pixels) of the cross-sections. By default, all vessels are selected.

(New in V2.0.0) Column 3 (④) asks you to select the reference (fixed) sequence. The options are based on the registration file names detected. If there is only one reference sequence (e.g., TOF), it is selected by default. Column 4 (⑤) asks you to select the sequence on which the centerlines are traced.

Select what you want and click OK. Then the command line window, you can monitor the extraction progress. Note that a larger height/width results in a larger scope (ROI, view) of cross-sections, but may also cause the software to respond more slowly.

Once the extraction is completed, each selected vessel will have a corresponding MOCHA folder named {vessel}_{ID} stored in the xsec folder in the 3D image folder, where {vessel} is the vessel name, and {ID} is a unique ID for that vessel. One MPR image folder will be automatically opened.

docs.title: 2D CASCADE folder
docs.text:
To open a 2D CASCADE folder:

  1. In the menubar, click File → Open Folder
  2. In the pop-up window, select a CASCADE project folder, which should contains QVS, QVJ and dcm files. Note that you need to select the folder itself, rather than the QVJ file in the folder.
  3. Wait for a while, the tool will read the images and contour information, then display the images.

New in V1.0.1

The tool support multiple project (.QVJ) files in the same folder. If it detects that, a pop-up window will ask the user to select one QVJ file to read. This is useful especially for some carotid datasets, in which there could be two QVJ files, for the left and right carotid arteries, respectively.

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
After opening a folder, the GUI will appear. Then you can start to use it.

There are splitters in the software window. For example:

You can drag them to adjust the size of different subwindows. You can even drag a splitter to make some subwindows disappear or appear again.

docs.title: Quickly open another folder
docs.text:
There is a folder tree on the left panel (figure below) that shows all folders at the same level of the currently opened folder.

To quickly open one of those folders, double click the folder name. A prompt window will ask whether you want to save your changes before opening another folder. Click one of the buttons:

  • Yes: save results and then close the software.
  • No: discard unsaved results, and then close the software.
  • Cancel: do not save results, nor close the software. In other words, nothing will happen.

This is very useful if you are reviewing multiple folders, such as different vessels of the same subject from VesselVoyager.

docs.title: Preprocessing
docs.text:
Assume you start with raw DICOM data of multiple image sequences. This page provides instructions about necessary initial steps to preprocess the raw data.

To start, load the raw data by click the button File → Open Raw Data. A prompt window will ask you to select the folder that contains those DICOM files.

docs.title: Sequence Selection
docs.text:
Once the folder is selected, the software starts to read the DICOMs and analyze what image sequences within.

A prompt window (example shown below) will display the sequence information.

On the left panel, there is a table (①). Each row corresponds to one image sequence.

  • Column 1 (Include): whether you want to include this image sequence for further processing and analysis. By default, all sequences are included. You can uncheck the checkboxes to exclude specific sequences.
  • Column 2 (Original Name): the original sequence names. This name is stored in the meta data of DICOM files. If you open the folder using RadiAnt, you will see the same name appears on the left panel of RadiAnt. The text in this column is not modifiable.
  • Column 3 (New Name): The new names you want to use for each image sequence. Double click to change the text. By default, the names are the same as the original names (except that "_" in the original name will be replaced by "-"). But changing the names makes further analysis clearer, e.g., you may want to change the name of sequence 1, 2, 3 to "pre-T1", "post-T1", and "TOF", respectively.

The right panel displays the image of currently selected sequence. You can change the display to another sequence by clicking its original name on the left panel. This image display helps you better identify what this sequence is. There is a small vertical line (②) below the image. Dragging it will change the slice displayed.

Once you have excluded sequences you don't need, and specify new names for the sequences you want to include, click OK. A prompt window will ask you to specify a patient folder to store the results. Usually this folder should be an empty folder (you may just create an empty folder in the prompt window) for this patient. All further analysis of the patient will be performed in this folder, including centerline tracing, MPR extraction, etc.

Once the patient folder is selected and the processing is done, you will see each image sequence is stored as an nii file in the folder, whose name is the new name you have specified (example shown below).

docs.title: Select Reference and Moving Sequences
docs.text:
Once the processing is done (the nii files are generated), the next step is image registration. A prompt window (example shown below) will automatically show to ask for registration information. If you cancelled this step by mistake or you just want to do image registration again for some specific image sequences, you can also trigger this prompt window by clicking the menubar, Preprocess → Registration.

Image registration is performed in a pairwise manner, namely each registration involves a reference (fixed) sequence and a moving sequence, and the registration will spatially align the moving sequence to the reference sequence by calculating a (rigid) spatial transformation. Specifying the reference and moving sequences is done by checking the checkboxes in column 2 and 3, respectively. Note that only one sequence can be selected as the reference, and all selected moving sequences will be registered to the reference.

Note

In practice, if we have \(N\) sequences, we usually need to do \(N-1\) registrations. It is recommended to select TOF MRA (if available) as the reference sequence, and other \(N-1\) sequences as the moving sequences.

The column 4 (Transform Same As) is designed for very special scenarios where some sequences may initially be registered during imaging. For example, the i2 and SNAP sequences in one single SNAP scan are usually assumed to be well registered because they are imaged together. In this case, one may want to select i2 as a moving image, and register it to the reference sequence TOF. For the other sequence SNAP, if we also select it as a moving sequence, then a separate registration will be performed between SNAP and TOF, which is not desirable. Instead, we may want to use the registration result of i2-to-TOF for SNAP-to-TOF, so that i2 and SNAP are still well registered after i2 is registered to to TOF. To this end, we need to select TOF as the reference sequence, i2 as the only one moving sequence, and then for SNAP, we select "i2" in the column 4, as shown below. This means "the spatial transformation of SNAP should be the same as the spatial transformation of i2".

docs.title: Set Initial Alignment
docs.text:
Once reference and moving sequences are selected, the next prompt window (shown below) will ask you to specify initial alignment parameters. The goal of this step is to specify a 3D point (spatial location) in each sequence, so that the selected locations of different sequences will be spatially aligned before the registration is started. This initial alignment is very important. It provides a rough initial registration effect so the following iterative automated registration is easier. If initial alignment is bad (e.g., the eye of one sequence is aligned with the circle of Willis of another sequence), then the following automated registration may fail.

The prompt window (example above) is divided into several sub-windows, each of which corresponds to the reference sequence or a moving sequence. The components in each sub-window includes:

  • ① Sequence name
  • ② A red crosshair indicates the point (3D spatial location) for this sequence.
  • ③ The coordinates of the point.
  • ④ A vertical line. Drag it to change the displayed 2D slice. The red crosshair appears only if the 3D point is located in the displayed 2D slice.
  • ⑤ If the displayed slice is not the one that contains the 3D point, then clicking this button to quickly change to the slice of the 3D point.
  • ⑥ Reset the 3D point to the default location, i.e., the center of the 3D image.

You can zoom in or out by scrolling up or down. You can click on any location of the image to change the 3D point to the clicked location.

It is recommended to change the 3D points for each sequence so these points are roughly at the same anatomical structure of the patient brain. A recommended structure is the tortuous part of the right ICA (because it is easy to find), as shown below.

docs.title: Automated Registration
docs.text:
Once the points are good, click OK to proceed. The automated registration will start. It is an iterative method. A prompt window with a progress bar will show the registration progress:

Note that registration is sequentially performed for each moving sequence, so you may see a prompt window disappears (registration finished for current moving sequence) and another one appears (registration started for next moving sequence). This procedure may take a few minutes.

Once registration is done for all moving sequences, the results will be stored as txt files in the same patient folder:

In the example above, since we have two moving sequences (pre-T1 and post-T1), there are two txt files storing the registration results for them separately. The name of the registration file indicates the moving sequence and reference sequence.

Once registration is finished, the following steps include

  1. Use VesselVoyager to trace centerlines on TOF, and generate centerline.yaml as the result. This is detailed in the VesselVoyager document.
  2. Use MOCHA to extract the MPR views for the sequences based on the centerline files and the registration files. To read the details, go to "Patient Folder Reading" on the left table of content of this webpage, then go to the section "3D Image Folder".

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: VesselVoyager is for tracing vessel centerlines and labeling centerlines as specific vessel types.

docs.title: V3.2.1
docs.text: Fix bugs: - Fix the bug that if there are loops in centerlines, saving will raise an error. - Fix the bug that if one converts the centerlines to be key point based and save it, the "are_key_point_based" entry in the yaml file is still "false", causing errors when the software opens it.

docs.title: V3.2.0
docs.text:
Functionalities:

  • Straightened window to show the longitudinal view of the centerline corresponding to a selected key point, selected curve, hovered key point or hovered curve.
    • A slider for rotating the view along the centerline. Hotkeys: Shift+E or Shift+Q.
    • Increase/decease the width (size of cross-sectional images) by the "-" or "+" buttons, the same as the buttons for the cross-sectional window.
    • Centerline key points shown in the window; click one key point to select it.
  • Convert non-key-point-based centerlines to key-point-based by clicking the menubar, "Tracing"->"To Key Point Based".
  • Add a new vessel type to the labeling table by click the menubar, "Labeling"->"Add Vessel Type". If the new type does not have two subtypes for the left and right sides, then add it directly through the prompt window by specifying the type name and color; otherwise, check the checkbox in the prompt window, and specify the type name (e.g., M4, rather than M4_L) and color for the left side, and the side-wise subtypes will be automatically added (e.g., M4_L and M4_R), and the color of the right-side subtype (e.g., M4_R) will be a darker version of the color of the left side.
  • Extend the function of keys "-" and "=": if a centerline is selected, press either of them to select the first or last key point of the centerline.
  • Pressing key "Q" or "E" has the same effect as pressing "-" or "=".
  • Add 3D navigation mode "Fly".
    • Change the mode through the menubar, "File"->"Settings". (restart the software to take effect)
    • Arrow keys, or WASD to move forward, backward, left and right; F and C keys move up and down; mouse dragging or the keys IKJL to control the pitch and yaw; space bar to brake; scroll to change moving speed; the camera auto-rotates to make the bottom point down, manual rolling can be performed using Q and E.

Bug fixes:

  • Fixed the bug that if a key point position is changed by shift + click, then the point will be deselected.
  • Fixed the bug that if the loaded image is a tif file, then changing histogram curve made 3D image totally black.

Misc:

  • Slightly increase the distance threshold for hovering key points and the curve in the histogram window to improve mouse hovering sensitivity.

docs.title: V3.1.1
docs.text:
Functionalities:

  • Ctrl+Shift+V: toggle the visibility of the 3D image.
  • Show cross-sectional image of hovered key or dense point, even if there is no selected key point.
  • If a key point is selected, select the previous or next key point of the same line by pressing "-" or "=".
  • Click the vessel type text in the labeling table to show or hide the centerlines of that type. Double-click the text to only show centerlines of that type, or show centerlines of all types. The text of hidden types will be darker than the shown ones.

Misc:

  • Substantially optimized opening and saving speed of non-key-point-based centerline files.
  • After using "Save As" to save the centerline results into a file, the opened file path will also be changed into that path. So the following "Save" actions will save the results to that path.
  • Slightly adjusted the colors of A2_L and A2_R to make them more distinguishable from each other.

Bug fixes:

  • Fixed the bug that if the coverage of the cross-sectional image is too large, then the crosshair is not at the center of the image or follows the mouse.

docs.title: Label Centerline Types
docs.text:
The labeling table on the right panel shows the information of vessel types.

The color blocks show the centerline curve and key point colors of each vessel type. If there are some centerline curves selected or hovered, the corresponding vessel types will be shown at the top of the labeling table, whose checkboxes are checked. For example, the following figure shows that the selected or hovered centerline curves are BA and VA_R.

Once some centerline curves are selected, you can click the checkbox of a vessel type in the labeling table to label the selected centerlines as that type. For example, the following video illustrates:

  1. Switch the selection priority to curve-first (curve priority > key point's) mode.
  2. Ctrl + drag to select multiple centerline curves.
  3. Click the checkbox of BA to label all selected centerlines as BA.

docs.title: Hover and select
docs.text:
Since each centerline contains two parts: a curve and several key points, the mouse hovering and selecting also work for them separately.

Since a key point is usually very close to a location on the curve, the software need to know whether you want to hover over the key point or the curve, if the mouse is around the key point. The button "Selection Priority" on the left panel is for this purpose:

By default, the priority of key point is larger than the curve. In this mode, if the mouse is close to both a key point and a curve, then the key point will be hovered. In this mode, the button is in blue (as shown above), and the text is "Ｏ > ～", where "Ｏ" means "key points", "～" means "curve", and ">" means "larger than".

The other mode is that the priority of curve is larger than key points. In this mode, if the mouse is close to both a key point and a curve, then the curve will be hovered. In this mode, the button is in orange (as shown below), and the text is "～ > Ｏ".

To switch between the two modes, click the button or press Ctrl + D.

docs.title: Hover over a centerline key point
docs.text: If a key point is hovered, the point will be highlighted in a relatively bright white color:

docs.title: Select centerline key points
docs.text:
If a key point is hovered, left-click to select it. Other things that are previously selected will be deselected at the same time. If only one key point is selected, press - or = to switch the selection to the previous or next key point of the same centerline.

To select multiple key points one by one, press and hold Ctrl , then hover over a key point and left-click. This is the same as selecting multiple files. During this procedure, if you left-click on a selected key point, it will be deselected.

To select multiple key points, you can also draw a region. Before doing this, first make sure the selection priority of key points is larger than curve (the button "Selection Priority" should be in blue). Press and hold Ctrl, then drag the mouse. This will draw a region based on the mouse trajectory, and select all the key points inside the region:

The selected key points will be shown in a very bright white color (brighter than hovered key point).

docs.title: Hover over a centerline curve
docs.text:
If a curve is hovered, the curve will be highlighted in a relatively bright white color, and the specific hovered location on the curve will be shown as a red point (smaller than centerline key points).

Sometimes multiple centerlines are close to each other, and you may find the hovered location or hovered centerline curve is not what you want. Then you can press Shift + Space to change the hovered location to another centerline location that is close to the mouse. You can confirm the change by the red point location or the highlighted curve.

docs.title: Select centerline curves
docs.text:
If a centerline curve is hovered, left-click to select it. Other things that are previously selected will be deselected at the same time.

To select multiple centerline curves one by one, press and hold Ctrl , then hover over a curve and left-click. This is the same as selecting multiple files. During this procedure, if you left-click on a selected curve, it will be deselected.

To select multiple curves, you can also draw a region. Before doing this, first make sure the selection priority of curve is larger than key points (the button "Selection Priority" should be in orange). Press and hold Ctrl, then drag the mouse. This will draw a region based on the mouse trajectory, and select all the curves inside the region:

The selected curves will be shown in a very bright white color (brighter than hovered curve).

docs.title: Cross-sectional window
docs.text:
The cross-sectional window is shown on the left panel. If a key point is selected, the cross-sectional image, which goes through this point and is perpendicular to the centerline curve that contains the point, will be shown in the window:

A semi-transparent blue square will be shown in the 3D window to indicate the cross-sectional plane.

In the cross-sectional window, if the mouse is outside the window, then a red crosshair will be shown to indicate the center of the cross-section (corresponding to the intersection point of the centerline curve and the cross-section). You can use it to quickly check whether the centerline location is at the lumen center.

In the cross-sectional window, if the mouse is inside the window, then a blue crosshair and a blue circle will be shown to indicate the mouse position. This is helpful for moving the selected key point, which will be explained in the following section.

If no key point is selected, then the cross-section is for the hovered key point or hovered centerline curve location (indicated by a red point, as mentioned before). If multiple key points are selected, then no cross-section will be shown.

docs.title: Move a key point
docs.text:
To move a key point to a new location, first you need to select it and only it. Then, there are two ways to change its location.

The first way is to use the cross-sectional window. This way is useful if you notice that a key point is not at the lumen center and want to move it to the center.

  1. Move the mouse to the desired location on the cross-sectional image.
  2. If the lumen is too small or too large, you can zoom in/out by scrolling up/down to make lumen boundary better match the blue circle.
  3. If the lumen is too large such that the cross-section only contains part of the lumen, you can click the button "+" in the upper right corner of the cross-sectional window to increase its coverage; similarly, click the button "-" to decrease the coverage.
  4. Shift + click. The selected key point will be moved to the 3D location that corresponds to the clicked 2D location of the cross-section.

The blue cross-sectional plane in the 3D window and the 2D image in the cross-sectional window will be both updated immediately to reflect the key point location change.

The second way is to use casted ray. This way is useful if the key point is far away from the lumen, such that the cross-sectional image does not even contain the lumen.

  1. Select only the key point.
  2. Shift + click on the location you want the key point to move to in the 3D window.
  3. Rotate the 3D image to observe the vessel from another direction, then you will see a cyan straight line that goes through the key point's new location. This line is the ray casted from the 2D mouse clicking location on the screen toward the 3D image. The ray is perpendicular to the screen. The location on the ray with the max image intensity is automatically calculated as the new key point location. By observing the vessel from another direction, you can determine whether the max intensity location on the casted ray is the location (lumen center) you want.
  4. If the new location of max intensity is still not what you want, then press and hold Shift, and move the mouse around the casted ray. The hovered location on the ray will be indicated by a small white point.
  5. Shift + click to change the key point location to the hovered location on the ray.

Therefore, by two clicks plus a dragging, you can move a key point to any 3D location you want in the 3D window. Note that click other places without dragging will make the ray disappear.

docs.title: Add a new key point on a centerline
docs.text:
You can add a new key point to an existing centerline. This is useful if you find the key point spacing is too large such that the centerline shape does not match the vessel shape correctly.

  1. Hover a centerline curve, such that a red point is shown to indicate the hovered location on the curve.
  2. Shift + A to add a key point at the hovered location.

Not applicable for non-key-point-based centerlines

If the centerline is not key-point-based, then you cannot add a new key point. This is because in this situation, the centerline is determined by dense point locations rather than interpolation based on key points, and each centerline only have two fake key points at the two endpoints. This will happen if the opened file is an SWC file, or a YAML file that was saved directly using an SWC file's centerline information. The function of converting such centerlines to key-point-based will be implemented in the future.

docs.title: Delete key points
docs.text:
You can delete key points of existing centerlines. This is useful if you find the key point spacing is too small such that the centerline shape is weird (caused by improper interpolation), or you have multiple centerlines share one key point (e.g., the bifurcation point) and you want to disconnect these centerlines.

  1. Select the key points you want to delete.
  2. Press Del or Backspace.

Alternatively, you can right-click a hovered key point to delete it.

Note that if after deleting, a centerline only has one key point, then that key point and the entire centerline will also be deleted. If a deleted key point is shared by multiple centerlines, then the key point will be deleted for all those centerlines.

docs.title: Split a centerline
docs.text:
You can split a centerline into two centerlines that share a key point at the split location. This is useful if you find the centerline actually contains two arteries, and you want to label two types. It is also useful if you want to change a centerline into two separate centerlines that does not share a key point at the split location, such that you can modify them separately (just delete the key point at the split location after splitting).

  1. Hover a centerline curve , such that a red point is shown to indicate the hovered location on the curve.
  2. Shift + S to split the centerline into two. A new key point will be added at the split location and shared by the two centerlines.

docs.title: Add new centerlines
docs.text:
To create new centerlines, first click the button "Add Points" on the left panel to enter the add-point mode. The hotkey is Ctrl + +a+.

Then, click the locations that you want to add key points at in the 3D window, following the order from one endpoint to the other endpoint of the centerline to create. the newly added key points will be shown in white.

You can also select existing key points in the add-point mode if you want the new centerline to be connected to existing centerlines.

If you click a location by mistake, you can undo the clicking by Ctrl + Z.

Then exist the add-point mode by clicking the button or pressing the hotkey again. New centerlines will be created based on the new key points you add and the existing key points you selected.

In the add-point mode, after clicking a new location to add a new key point, you can drag the image to observe the vessel from another direction, then the casted ray will be shown and you can change the newly added key point location in the same way as mentioned in the section "Move a key point" above. In short, Shift + click to change the location to the hovered location on the casted ray, as shown below:

Pay attention to the order of clicking

New centerlines will be created based on the order of your clicks on new locations and existing key points.

Existing centerlines may be automatically split

During the add-point mode, if you clicked some existing key points that are not the endpoints of existing centerlines, then those existing centerlines will be split into several centerlines based on the clicked key points. This is because the software defines individual centerlines by bifurcations.

You can form a loop

  • You cannot consecutively click the same location (the key point will disappear or deselected).
  • Still, you can click the same location as long as you do not click it twice consecutively. Therefore, you can create a centerline loop. This is useful, for example, for tracing the centerline of circle of Willis.

docs.title: Open and Save
docs.text: The buttons for opening and saving are on the left panel:

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
Two types of files can be opened: image file and centerline file. To open a file, click the button "Open".

An image file is a NIfTI file (extension name: .nii or .nii.gz) or a TIFF file (extension name: .tif).

A centerline file is a YAML file (extension name: .yaml or .yml) or an SWC file (extension name: .swc). The YAML file should follow VesselVoyager's centerline format; the SWC file should follow iCafe's centerline format.

The opened file paths are displayed in the upper center of the window, like this:

docs.title: Save
docs.text:
To save the centerline result to the currently opened centerline file, click the button "Save". The hotkey is Ctrl + S.

To save the centerline result to another file, click the button "Save As", then a prompt window will ask for a file path to save the result, and once saving is finished, the opened file path will be changed into the new path.

Cannot save to a SWC file

If the opened centerline file is an SWC file, then the button "Save" will be disabled (cannot be clicked). This is because the software always saves the result into a YAML file.

Once saving is finished, the status bar at the bottom of the software window will show a message like this:

docs.title: Image
docs.text:
Once an image file is opened, you can observe the 3D image in the middle window (called the 3D window). The image is shown in the maximum intensity projection (MIP) mode, that is, a larger pixel value corresponds to a larger brightness.

To hide or show the 3D image, use the hotkey Ctrl + Shift + V. This is useful if you want to only observe the centerlines more clearly.

docs.title: Histogram Window
docs.text:
The intensity histogram window is in the lower left corner of the window (shown below). This is particularly useful for enhancing the visibility of certain (e.g., distal) vessels. It may even be useful for observing the vessels on black-blood images.

The histogram shows the pixel intensity distribution of the opened image, after clipping negative intensities to 0. The x-axis is the intensity value.

The red line defines the mapping between pixel intensities and brightness in the MIP view. The y-axis is the brightness (0-1). By default, it is just a straight line from \((0, 0)\) to \((\text{max_intensity}, 1)\), which means the intensity 0 corresponds to brightness 0 (transparent), and the max intensity corresponds to brightness 1 (max brightness).

The red line's shape is controlled by red key points. You can change the line shape by:

  • Drag a key point to move it
  • Drag starting from any location on the red line to add a new key point and move it.
  • Right-click a key point (except for the two endpoints) to delete it.

Note that the two endpoints' x coordinates cannot be changed.

Once you release the mouse button after dragging or right-clicking, new mapping will be calculated based on the red line shape to change the pixel brightness. This process takes about 2 seconds. Once it is done, you can observe the effect by moving the mouse into the 3D window:

docs.title: Centerlines
docs.text: Once a centerline file is opened, you can observe the centerlines in the 3D window. If a 3D image is also shown, you can observe them together:

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Each shown centerline has two parts: a curve and several key points that defines the curve, like this:

The number of key points must be at least 2. If the number is smaller than 4, then the curve is piecewise linear (not smooth); otherwise, the curve is smooth (calculated by cubic spline interpolation based on all key points).

docs.title: Color
docs.text:
The color of the centerline (including the curve and key points) is determined by its vessel type. The correspondences between colors and types are shown in the labeling table on the right panel:

For example, the figure above shows that the centerline with the type ICA_L (left internal carotid artery) is in orange.

Some artery like ICA has two types, i.e., left (L) and right (R) sides. The left and right side colors of the same artery are different in brightness (the right-side type is darker). This is very useful if you want to quickly check if the left and right sides of the same artery have been labeled correctly.

There is a type "unassigned" (in green) for the centerlines that have no labeling information. It is also the default type if you add a new centerline.

docs.title: Hide
docs.text:
You can hide or show certain types of centerlines. This is useful if you want to observe the image or certain types of centerlines more clearly.

  • To hide or show all centerlines, press Shift + V.
  • To hide or show the centerlines of a specific type, click the text of type in the labeling table.
  • To only show the centerlines of a specific type (hide all other centerlines), or show all centerlines, double-click the text of the type in the labeling table.

The text of hidden types in the labeling table will be shown in dark gray. For example, the figure below shows that the centerlines with types ICA_L or BA are hidden.

docs.title: 3D Navigation
docs.text:
You can observe the 3D image and/or centerlines from different directions and scales. There are two typical navigation modes: arcball and fly. We currently support the arcball mode; the fly mode will be supported in the future.

Arcball mode: - Left-drag: orbits the view around its center point. - Right-drag or scroll: zoom in or out. - Shift + left-drag: translate the center point. - Shift + right-drag: change the field of view (FOV).

There is a XYZ-axis shown in the 3D window to indicate the center point of the camera, which can help better determine the navigation you want. You can see the XYZ-axis by zooming in enough:
